description: Main physical definitions that are not part of the main units.

words.name: second
words.description: Ambiguous word: either a unit to measure a duration or an ordinal position in a ranking (first, second, third, ...)

words.name: force
words.description: In physics, a force is an influence that can change the motion of an object; it has both magnitude and direction and is measured in newton.

words.name: mass
words.description: Mass is the quantity of matter in a body and a measure of its resistance to acceleration (inertia) when a force is applied; the SI unit is the kilogram.

words.name: energy
words.description: Energy is the quantitative property that is transferred to a body or system to perform work or to heat it; the SI unit is the joule.

words.name: power
words.description: Power is the amount of energy transferred or converted per unit time; the SI unit is the watt.

words.name: pressure
words.description: Pressure is the force applied perpendicular to the surface of an object per unit area; the SI unit is the pascal.

words.name: voltage
words.description: Voltage, also called electric potential difference, is the difference in electric potential between two points; the SI unit is the volt.

words.name: momentum
words.description: In Newtonian mechanics, momentum is the product of the mass and velocity of an object; it is a vector quantity.

words.name: impulse
words.description: In classical mechanics, impulse is the change in momentum of an object; it equals the integral of force over the time interval for which it acts.

words.name: work
words.description: In physics, work is the energy transferred to or from an object via the application of force along a displacement.

words.name: torque
words.description: In physics and mechanics, torque is the rotational equivalent of linear force; it is also referred to as the moment of force.

words.name: inertia
words.description: Inertia is the tendency of an object to maintain its state of motion unless acted upon by a force.

words.name: friction
words.description: Friction is the force resisting the relative motion of solid surfaces, fluid layers, and material elements sliding against each other.

words.name: gravity
words.description: In physics, gravity is a fundamental interaction which causes mutual attraction between all things that have mass.

words.name: density
words.description: quantity per unit area or volume

words.name: temperature
words.description: Temperature is a physical quantity that expresses quantitatively the perceptions of hotness and coldness.

words.name: heat
words.description: In thermodynamics, heat is the thermal energy transferred between systems due to a temperature difference.

words.name: entropy
words.description: Entropy is a scientific concept that is most commonly associated with a state of disorder, randomness, or uncertainty in a thermodynamic system.

words.name: enthalpy
words.description: Enthalpy is the sum of a thermodynamic system's internal energy and the product of its pressure and volume.

words.name: current
words.description: An electric current is a flow of charged particles, such as electrons or ions, moving through an electrical conductor or space.

words.name: resistance
words.description: The electrical resistance of an object is a measure of its opposition to the flow of electric current.

words.name: capacitance
words.description: Capacitance is the capability of a material object or device to store electric charge.

words.name: inductance
words.description: Inductance is the tendency of an electrical conductor to oppose a change in the electric current flowing through it.

words.name: permittivity
words.description: In electromagnetism, the permittivity is a measure of the electric polarizability of a dielectric.

words.name: permeability
words.description: In electromagnetism, permeability is the measure of magnetization that a material obtains in response to an applied magnetic field.

words.name: wavelength
words.description: In physics and mathematics, wavelength is the spatial period of a periodic wave, the distance over which the wave's shape repeats.

words.name: wave
words.description: In physics, a wave is a propagating dynamic disturbance of one or more quantities.

words.name: photon
words.description: A photon is an elementary particle that is a quantum of the electromagnetic field, including electromagnetic radiation such as light and radio waves.

words.name: electron
words.description: The electron is a subatomic particle with a negative one elementary electric charge.

words.name: proton
words.description: A proton is a stable subatomic particle, symbol p, with a positive electric charge of +1 e elementary charge.

words.name: neutron
words.description: The neutron is a subatomic particle, symbol n, which has a neutral charge, and a mass slightly greater than that of a proton.

words.name: atom
words.description: Atoms are the basic particles of the chemical elements and the fundamental building blocks of ordinary matter.

words.name: nucleus
words.description: The atomic nucleus is the small, dense region consisting of protons and neutrons at the center of an atom.

words.name: spring
words.description: A spring is an elastic object that stores mechanical energy and is typically used as a mechanical component.

words.name: pendulum
words.description: A pendulum is a weight suspended from a pivot so that it can swing freely.

words.name: lens
words.description: A lens is a transmissive optical device that focuses or disperses a light beam by means of refraction.

words.name: refraction
words.description: In physics, refraction is the redirection of a wave as it passes from one medium to another.

words.name: reflection
words.description: Reflection is the change in direction of a wavefront at an interface between two different media so that the wavefront returns into the medium from which it originated.

words.name: field
words.description: magnetic field strength of the MRI scanner

words.name: phase
words.description: one distinguishable segment of a procedure

words.name: constant
words.description: fixed and well-defined number

words.name: Coulomb
words.description: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb was a French officer, engineer, and physicist; the SI unit of electric charge and Coulomb's law are named after him.

words.name: Ohm
words.description: Georg Simon Ohm was a German physicist and mathematician known for Ohm's law.

words.name: Newton
words.description: Sir Isaac Newton was an English mathematician, physicist, astronomer and author widely recognised as one of the greatest mathematicians and most influential scientists of all time.

words.name: Einstein
words.description: Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist who is widely held to be one of the greatest and most influential scientists of all time.

words.name: Hooke
words.description: Robert Hooke was an English polymath who was active as a scientist, natural philosopher and architect, and Hooke's law is named after him.

words.name: Bernoulli
words.description: Daniel Bernoulli was a Swiss mathematician and physicist who made important contributions to fluid mechanics.

words.name: Snell
words.description: Willebrord Snellius was a Dutch astronomer and mathematician; the law of refraction is named after him.

words.name: Planck
words.description: Max Planck was a German theoretical physicist whose discovery of energy quanta won him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1918.

words.name: deBroglie
words.description: Louis de Broglie was a French physicist and aristocrat known for his contributions to quantum theory.

words.name: Stefan
words.description: Josef Stefan was a Slovene physicist, mathematician, and poet of the Austrian Empire; the Stefan-Boltzmann law is partly named after him.

words.name: Wien
words.description: Wilhelm Wien was a German physicist who studied radiation and electromagnetism, winning the 1911 Nobel Prize in Physics.

words.name: Schrödinger
words.description: Erwin Schrödinger was an Austrian-Irish physicist who developed fundamental results in quantum theory.

words.name: Heisenberg
words.description: Werner Heisenberg was a German theoretical physicist and one of the main pioneers of the theory of quantum mechanics.

words.name: Faraday
words.description: Michael Faraday was an English scientist who contributed to the study of electromagnetism and electrochemistry.

words.name: Lorentz
words.description: Hendrik Lorentz was a Dutch physicist who shared the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pieter Zeeman.

words.name: Ampère
words.description: André-Marie Ampère was a French physicist and mathematician who was one of the founders of the science of classical electromagnetism.

words.name: Gauss
words.description: Carl Friedrich Gauss was a German mathematician and physicist who made significant contributions to many fields.

words.name: G
words.description: G is the gravitational constant, an empirical physical constant involved in the calculation of gravitational effects.

words.name: c
words.description: c is the speed of light in vacuum, a universal physical constant exactly equal to 299792458 m/s.

words.name: h
words.description: h is the Planck constant, a fundamental physical constant that relates the energy carried by a photon to its frequency.

words.name: ℏ
words.description: ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, equal to the Planck constant divided by 2π.

words.name: kB
words.description: kB is the Boltzmann constant, the proportionality factor that relates the average kinetic energy of particles in a gas with the thermodynamic temperature of the gas.

words.name: NA
words.description: NA is the Avogadro constant, the proportionality factor that relates the number of constituent particles in a sample with the amount of substance in that sample.

words.name: σ
words.description: σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, the constant of proportionality in the Stefan-Boltzmann law.

words.name: ε0
words.description: ε0 is the vacuum permittivity, the absolute permittivity of free space.

words.name: μ0
words.description: μ0 is the vacuum permeability, the magnetic permeability of classical vacuum.

words.name: ke
words.description: ke is the Coulomb constant, the proportionality constant in Coulomb's law.

words.name: first
words.description: the ordinal describing the position one in a sequence, e.g. a first law

words.name: thermodynamics
words.description: the branch of physics that deals with heat, work, temperature and the statistical behaviour of systems.

words.name: electromagnetism
words.description: the branch of physics that deals with electric and magnetic phenomena and their interaction

words.name: optics
words.description: the branch of physics that deals with light and its interaction with matter

triples.name: quantum mechanics
triples.description: the branch of physics that describes matter and energy at atomic and subatomic scales

triples.name: time unit
triples.description: a unit to measure a duration, used to disambiguate words like 'second' that also have a non-time meaning

triples.name: ranking number
triples.description: an ordinal position in a ranking (first, second, third, ...), used to disambiguate words like 'second' that also are a time unit

triples.name: second (ranking)
triples.description: the ranking-number reading of the ambiguous word 'second'; displayed as 'second' with 'ranking number' shown only in the tooltip

triples.name: first law
triples.description: a law that is the first in a numbered set of laws

triples.name: second law
triples.description: a law that is the second in a numbered set of laws

triples.name: kinetic energy
triples.description: In physics, the kinetic energy of an object is the form of energy that it possesses due to its motion.

triples.name: potential energy
triples.description: In physics, potential energy is the energy held by an object because of its position relative to other objects, stresses within itself, or other factors.

triples.name: internal energy
triples.description: The internal energy of a thermodynamic system is the energy contained within it; it is the energy necessary to create or prepare the system in any given internal state.

triples.name: angular momentum
triples.description: In physics, angular momentum is the rotational analog of linear momentum.

triples.name: centripetal acceleration
triples.description: Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration of an object moving in a circular path, directed toward the centre of the circle.

triples.name: moment of inertia
triples.description: The moment of inertia is a quantity expressing a body's tendency to resist angular acceleration; it is the sum of the products of the mass of each particle in the body with the square of its distance from the axis of rotation.

triples.name: Newton's second law
triples.description: Newton's second law of motion states that the net force on an object is equal to the rate of change of its linear momentum with respect to time.

triples.name: Newton's law of gravitation
triples.description: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that every particle attracts every other particle in the universe with a force which is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.

triples.name: Hooke's law
triples.description: In physics, Hooke's law is an empirical law which states that the force needed to extend or compress a spring by some distance scales linearly with respect to that distance.

triples.name: Coulomb's law
triples.description: Coulomb's law is an experimental law of physics that calculates the amount of force between two electrically charged particles at rest.

triples.name: Ohm's law
triples.description: Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points.

triples.name: Snell's law
triples.description: Snell's law is a formula used to describe the relationship between the angles of incidence and refraction, when referring to light or other waves passing through a boundary between two different isotropic media.

triples.name: Bernoulli's equation
triples.description: Bernoulli's principle states that an increase in the speed of a fluid occurs simultaneously with a decrease in static pressure or a decrease in the fluid's potential energy.

triples.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
triples.description: The Stefan-Boltzmann law describes the power radiated from a black body in terms of its temperature.

triples.name: Wien's displacement law
triples.description: Wien's displacement law states that the black-body radiation curve for different temperatures will peak at different wavelengths that are inversely proportional to the temperature.

triples.name: Faraday's law
triples.description: Faraday's law of induction is a basic law of electromagnetism predicting how a magnetic field will interact with an electric circuit to produce an electromotive force.

triples.name: Lorentz force
triples.description: In electromagnetism, the Lorentz force is the force exerted on a charged particle moving with velocity through an electric and magnetic field.

triples.name: Ampère's law
triples.description: Ampère's circuital law relates the integrated magnetic field around a closed loop to the electric current passing through the loop.

triples.name: Gauss's law
triples.description: In physics, Gauss's law relates the distribution of electric charge to the resulting electric field.

triples.name: de Broglie relation
triples.description: The de Broglie hypothesis proposes that all matter exhibits wave-like behaviour, and the de Broglie wavelength of a particle is inversely proportional to its momentum.

triples.name: Planck-Einstein relation
triples.description: The Planck-Einstein relation states that the energy of a photon is proportional to its frequency.

triples.name: Heisenberg uncertainty principle
triples.description: In quantum mechanics, the uncertainty principle is any of a variety of mathematical inequalities asserting a fundamental limit to the accuracy with which the values for certain pairs of physical quantities of a particle can be predicted from initial conditions.

triples.name: Schrödinger equation
triples.description: The Schrödinger equation is a linear partial differential equation that governs the wave function of a quantum-mechanical system.

triples.name: Einstein mass-energy equivalence
triples.description: In physics, mass-energy equivalence is the relationship between mass and energy in a system's rest frame, where the two quantities differ only by a multiplicative constant and the units of measurement.

triples.name: ideal gas law
triples.description: The ideal gas law is the equation of state of a hypothetical ideal gas, relating its pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of substance.

triples.name: first law of thermodynamics
triples.description: The first law of thermodynamics is a formulation of the law of conservation of energy in the context of thermodynamic processes.

triples.name: second law of thermodynamics
triples.description: The second law of thermodynamics is a physical law based on universal empirical observation concerning heat and energy interconversions.

triples.name: specific heat
triples.description: In thermodynamics, the specific heat capacity of a substance is the heat capacity of a sample of the substance divided by the mass of the sample.

triples.name: electric field
triples.description: An electric field is the physical field that surrounds electrically charged particles.

triples.name: magnetic field
triples.description: A magnetic field is a vector field that describes the magnetic influence on moving electric charges, electric currents, and magnetic materials.

triples.name: magnetic flux
triples.description: In physics, specifically electromagnetism, the magnetic flux through a surface is the surface integral of the magnetic field component perpendicular to the surface.

triples.name: electric potential
triples.description: The electric potential at a point in a static electric field is the work needed per unit of charge to move a positive test charge from a reference point to that specific point.

formulas.name: definition of newton
formulas.description: the SI unit of force, the force that accelerates a mass of one kilogram by one metre per second squared

formulas.name: definition of pascal
formulas.description: the SI unit of pressure, one newton per square metre; the air pressure at sea level is about 100000 pascal

formulas.name: definition of watt
formulas.description: the SI unit of power, one joule of energy per second

formulas.name: definition of coulomb
formulas.description: the SI unit of electric charge, the charge that a current of one ampere carries in one second

formulas.name: definition of volt
formulas.description: the SI unit of voltage, the potential difference that delivers one watt of power at a current of one ampere

formulas.name: definition of velocity
formulas.description: the distance covered per unit of time, e.g. in metres per second

formulas.name: average velocity
formulas.description: the change of position divided by the time it took, the average speed over an interval regardless of how the speed varied in between

formulas.name: definition of acceleration
formulas.description: the change of velocity per unit of time, e.g. in metres per second squared

formulas.name: kinematics final velocity
formulas.description: the velocity after a time of constant acceleration, the starting velocity plus the acceleration multiplied by the time

formulas.name: kinematics displacement
formulas.description: the position after a time of constant acceleration, from the starting position, the starting velocity and the acceleration, e.g. the fall distance of a dropped stone
formulas.latex: x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2} a t^2

formulas.name: kinematics velocity squared
formulas.description: the velocity after a distance of constant acceleration without knowing the time, e.g. the speed of a car at the end of a braking distance

formulas.name: average velocity from endpoints
formulas.description: the average velocity during a constant acceleration is the mean of the starting and the final velocity

formulas.name: definition of Newton's second law
formulas.description: the force on a body is its mass multiplied by its acceleration, the basic law of mechanics that links forces to motion

formulas.name: Newton's second law momentum form
formulas.description: the force on a body is the change of its momentum per unit of time, the general form of the second law that also holds for a changing mass

formulas.name: weight
formulas.description: the gravitational force on a body, its mass multiplied by the gravitational acceleration of about 9.81 metres per second squared on earth

formulas.name: definition of Newton's law of gravitation
formulas.description: the attraction between two masses, proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance

formulas.name: gravitational potential energy near surface
formulas.description: the energy stored by lifting a mass to a height near the surface of the earth, the work needed against the weight

formulas.name: gravitational potential energy general
formulas.description: the potential energy of two masses at any distance, negative because energy is needed to separate them completely, e.g. for a satellite orbit or an escape velocity

formulas.name: friction force
formulas.description: the force that resists the sliding of two surfaces, the friction coefficient of the material pair multiplied by the force pressing the surfaces together

formulas.name: definition of linear momentum
formulas.description: the momentum of a moving body, its mass multiplied by its velocity, which is conserved in collisions

formulas.name: impulse momentum theorem
formulas.description: a force acting for a time changes the momentum of a body by the impulse, the force multiplied by the time; why airbags stretch the stopping time to reduce the force

formulas.name: definition of kinetic energy
formulas.description: the energy of a moving body, half its mass multiplied by the square of its velocity; doubling the speed quadruples the energy

formulas.name: work done by force
formulas.description: the energy transferred by a force that moves a body, the force multiplied by the distance in the direction of the force

formulas.name: work energy theorem
formulas.description: the work done on a body equals the change of its kinetic energy

formulas.name: power from work
formulas.description: the power of a process, the work done or energy transferred per unit of time

formulas.name: power from force and velocity
formulas.description: the power needed to move a body against a force at a velocity, e.g. the engine power of a car against the air resistance

formulas.name: definition of Hooke's law
formulas.description: the restoring force of a spring is proportional to how far it is stretched or compressed, with the spring constant k as the stiffness

formulas.name: definition of elastic potential energy
formulas.description: the energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring, half the spring constant multiplied by the square of the displacement

formulas.name: spring period
formulas.description: the time of one full oscillation of a mass on a spring, longer for a heavier mass and shorter for a stiffer spring, independent of the amplitude

formulas.name: simple pendulum period
formulas.description: the time of one full swing of a pendulum for small angles, which depends only on its length and the gravitational acceleration, not on its mass

formulas.name: definition of angular velocity
formulas.description: the angle turned per unit of time, in radians per second, the rotational counterpart of the velocity

formulas.name: angular velocity from frequency
formulas.description: the angular velocity of a rotation or oscillation from its frequency, two pi radians per full turn

formulas.name: tangential velocity
formulas.description: the speed of a point on a rotating body along its circular path, the angular velocity multiplied by the distance from the axis

formulas.name: definition of centripetal acceleration
formulas.description: the acceleration towards the centre that keeps a body on a circular path, the square of the speed divided by the radius

formulas.name: definition of centripetal force
formulas.description: the force towards the centre needed to keep a mass on a circular path, e.g. the friction of the tyres in a curve

formulas.name: definition of angular momentum
formulas.description: the rotational counterpart of the momentum, the moment of inertia multiplied by the angular velocity, which is conserved when no torque acts, e.g. a spinning skater pulling in the arms

formulas.name: definition of torque
formulas.description: the turning effect of a force, the force multiplied by the lever arm and the sine of the angle between them, e.g. of a wrench on a bolt

formulas.name: torque from angular acceleration
formulas.description: Newton's second law for rotations, the torque is the moment of inertia multiplied by the angular acceleration

formulas.name: definition of rotational kinetic energy
formulas.description: the energy of a rotating body, half the moment of inertia multiplied by the square of the angular velocity, e.g. of a flywheel

formulas.name: definition of density
formulas.description: the mass per unit of volume of a substance, e.g. 1000 kilograms per cubic metre for water

formulas.name: pressure from force and area
formulas.description: the force per unit of area on a surface, in pascal; the same force on a smaller area gives a higher pressure, e.g. a needle

formulas.name: hydrostatic pressure
formulas.description: the pressure at a depth in a liquid caused by the weight of the liquid above, about one bar more for every 10 metres of water

formulas.name: buoyant force
formulas.description: the upward force on a body in a fluid by Archimedes' principle, the weight of the fluid that the body displaces

formulas.name: definition of Bernoulli's equation
formulas.description: the energy conservation of a flowing fluid: the pressure, the kinetic energy per volume and the potential energy per volume add up to a constant along a streamline, so a faster flow has a lower pressure

formulas.name: continuity equation
formulas.description: the volume flow of an incompressible fluid is the same everywhere in a pipe, so the fluid speeds up where the cross-section narrows

formulas.name: Celsius to Kelvin
formulas.description: convert a temperature in degrees Celsius to the absolute temperature in kelvin, which starts at the absolute zero of -273.15 degrees Celsius

formulas.name: definition of ideal gas law
formulas.description: the relation of the pressure, the volume, the amount and the temperature of a gas, a good approximation for most gases at everyday conditions

formulas.name: ideal gas Boltzmann form
formulas.description: the ideal gas law written with the number of particles and the Boltzmann constant instead of the amount in moles and the gas constant

formulas.name: definition of specific heat
formulas.description: the heat needed to change the temperature of a mass, the mass multiplied by the specific heat capacity of the material and the temperature change

formulas.name: definition of first law of thermodynamics
formulas.description: the energy conservation for heat: the internal energy of a system changes by the heat added minus the work the system does

formulas.name: entropy change
formulas.description: the change of entropy of a system when heat is added reversibly at a temperature, the heat divided by the absolute temperature

formulas.name: Carnot efficiency
formulas.description: the highest possible efficiency of a heat engine working between a hot and a cold temperature, one minus the ratio of the cold to the hot absolute temperature

formulas.name: thermal linear expansion
formulas.description: how much the length of a body grows when it is heated, the expansion coefficient of the material multiplied by the length and the temperature change, e.g. of a bridge in summer

formulas.name: average kinetic energy of gas particle
formulas.description: the average energy of motion of a particle in an ideal gas, which depends only on the absolute temperature, the link between temperature and molecular motion

formulas.name: RMS molecular speed
formulas.description: the typical speed of the particles of a gas, the root mean square, which grows with the temperature and is lower for heavier particles, e.g. about 500 metres per second for air at room temperature

formulas.name: definition of Stefan-Boltzmann law
formulas.description: the power radiated by a hot surface grows with the fourth power of its absolute temperature, which sets the temperature of stars and planets

formulas.name: definition of Wien's displacement law
formulas.description: the wavelength at which a hot body radiates most is inversely proportional to its temperature, why a hotter star looks blue and a cooler one red

formulas.name: definition of Coulomb's law
formulas.description: the force between two electric charges, proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their distance, like gravity but attracting or repelling

formulas.name: electric field of point charge
formulas.description: the strength of the electric field around a point charge, the force per unit of test charge, falling with the square of the distance

formulas.name: electric force on charge
formulas.description: the force on a charge in an electric field, the charge multiplied by the field strength

formulas.name: electric potential of point charge
formulas.description: the electric potential at a distance from a point charge, the work per unit of charge to bring a test charge there from infinity, falling with the distance

formulas.name: electric potential energy
formulas.description: the energy stored in the arrangement of two charges at a distance, positive for like charges that repel and negative for unlike charges that attract

formulas.name: voltage from electric potential
formulas.description: the voltage or electric potential is the potential energy per unit of charge, in volts

formulas.name: definition of Ohm's law
formulas.description: the voltage across a conductor is the current through it multiplied by its resistance, the basic relation of electric circuits

formulas.name: electric power
formulas.description: the power delivered by an electric current, the voltage multiplied by the current, in watts

formulas.name: power dissipated by resistor
formulas.description: the heat produced in a resistor per unit of time, the square of the current multiplied by the resistance, e.g. in a heating wire

formulas.name: resistance from resistivity
formulas.description: the resistance of a wire from the resistivity of its material, its length and its cross-section; a longer or thinner wire has a higher resistance

formulas.name: resistors in series
formulas.description: the total resistance of resistors connected one after the other is the sum of the single resistances

formulas.name: resistors in parallel
formulas.description: the reciprocal of the total resistance of resistors connected side by side is the sum of the reciprocals, so the total is smaller than the smallest single resistance

formulas.name: current as charge rate
formulas.description: the electric current is the charge that flows through a cross-section per unit of time, in amperes

formulas.name: definition of capacitance
formulas.description: how much charge a capacitor stores per volt of voltage across it, in farads

formulas.name: energy stored in capacitor
formulas.description: the energy held in the electric field of a charged capacitor, half the capacitance multiplied by the square of the voltage

formulas.name: parallel plate capacitance
formulas.description: the capacitance of two parallel plates in vacuum, larger for bigger plates and a smaller gap between them

formulas.name: capacitors in parallel
formulas.description: the total capacitance of capacitors connected side by side is the sum of the single capacitances, the opposite of resistors

formulas.name: capacitors in series
formulas.description: the reciprocal of the total capacitance of capacitors connected one after the other is the sum of the reciprocals

formulas.name: definition of Lorentz force
formulas.description: the total force on a moving charge in an electric and a magnetic field, the electric part plus the magnetic part that depends on the velocity

formulas.name: magnetic force on charge
formulas.description: the force on a charge moving through a magnetic field, largest when it moves across the field and zero when it moves along it; it bends the path but does no work

formulas.name: magnetic force on current
formulas.description: the force on a wire carrying a current in a magnetic field, the principle of the electric motor

formulas.name: magnetic field around wire
formulas.description: the strength of the magnetic field around a long straight wire, proportional to the current and falling with the distance from the wire

formulas.name: magnetic field in solenoid
formulas.description: the nearly uniform magnetic field inside a long coil, proportional to the current and the number of turns per unit of length

formulas.name: definition of magnetic flux
formulas.description: the amount of magnetic field passing through a surface, the field strength multiplied by the area and the cosine of the angle to the surface normal

formulas.name: definition of Faraday's law
formulas.description: a changing magnetic flux through a loop induces a voltage that opposes the change, the principle of the generator and the transformer

formulas.name: inductance EMF
formulas.description: the voltage a coil induces in itself when the current through it changes, proportional to its inductance and the rate of the change

formulas.name: energy stored in inductor
formulas.description: the energy held in the magnetic field of a coil carrying a current, half the inductance multiplied by the square of the current

formulas.name: speed of light from permittivity and permeability
formulas.description: the speed of light in vacuum follows from the two constants of electricity and magnetism, the discovery of Maxwell that light is an electromagnetic wave

formulas.name: wave speed
formulas.description: the speed of a wave is its frequency multiplied by its wavelength, valid for sound, water and light waves

formulas.name: period from frequency
formulas.description: the time of one oscillation is the reciprocal of the number of oscillations per second

formulas.name: definition of Snell's law
formulas.description: how light bends when it passes from one medium into another, the product of the refractive index and the sine of the angle to the normal is the same on both sides

formulas.name: index of refraction
formulas.description: how much slower light travels in a medium than in vacuum, e.g. about 1.33 for water and 1.5 for glass

formulas.name: thin lens equation
formulas.description: the relation between the focal length of a lens, the distance of the object and the distance of the image, used to find where a lens forms a sharp image

formulas.name: magnification
formulas.description: how many times larger the image of a lens is than the object, the ratio of the image distance to the object distance, negative for an upside-down image

formulas.name: Doppler effect sound
formulas.description: the change of the pitch of a sound when the source or the listener moves, higher when they approach and lower when they move apart, e.g. a passing siren

formulas.name: photon energy
formulas.description: the energy of a single light quantum, the Planck constant multiplied by the frequency, so blue light carries more energy per photon than red light

formulas.name: photon energy from wavelength
formulas.description: the energy of a photon from its wavelength instead of its frequency, shorter wavelengths carry more energy

formulas.name: photon momentum
formulas.description: the momentum of a photon, the Planck constant divided by the wavelength, which lets light push on matter, e.g. a solar sail

formulas.name: de Broglie wavelength
formulas.description: every moving particle has a wavelength, the Planck constant divided by its momentum, the wave nature of matter used in electron microscopes

formulas.name: Heisenberg uncertainty position momentum
formulas.description: the position and the momentum of a particle cannot both be known exactly, the product of their uncertainties has a lower limit set by the reduced Planck constant

formulas.name: Heisenberg uncertainty energy time
formulas.description: the energy of a state and the time it exists cannot both be exact, so a short-lived particle has an uncertain mass

formulas.name: reduced Planck constant
formulas.description: the Planck constant divided by two pi, the natural unit of angular momentum in quantum mechanics

formulas.name: photoelectric effect
formulas.description: the kinetic energy of an electron knocked out of a metal by light, the photon energy minus the work needed to free the electron, Einstein's explanation of the quantum nature of light

formulas.name: mass-energy equivalence
formulas.description: the energy contained in a mass at rest, the mass multiplied by the square of the speed of light, the source of the energy of nuclear reactions

formulas.name: Lorentz factor
formulas.description: the factor of special relativity by which time slows and lengths shrink for a moving body, close to one at everyday speeds and growing without limit near the speed of light

formulas.name: time dilation
formulas.description: a clock moving relative to an observer runs slower by the Lorentz factor, measurable for satellites and fast particles

formulas.name: length contraction
formulas.description: a body moving relative to an observer appears shorter in the direction of motion by the Lorentz factor

formulas.name: relativistic energy
formulas.description: the total energy of a moving body, the rest energy multiplied by the Lorentz factor, which includes the kinetic energy

formulas.name: relativistic momentum
formulas.description: the momentum of a fast body, the classical momentum multiplied by the Lorentz factor, which is why nothing with mass can reach the speed of light

formulas.name: energy momentum relation
formulas.description: the relation between the total energy, the momentum and the rest mass of a particle in special relativity, which also holds for massless photons

formulas.name: radioactive decay
formulas.description: the number of radioactive nuclei left after a time, falling exponentially with the decay constant of the isotope

formulas.name: half-life
formulas.description: the time until half of the radioactive nuclei have decayed, the natural logarithm of 2 divided by the decay constant, e.g. 5730 years for carbon-14

formulas.name: amount of substance from particles
formulas.description: the amount of substance in moles from the number of particles, using the Avogadro constant of about 6.022 times 10^23 particles per mole

formulas.name: Bohr radius energy levels
formulas.description: the energy of the electron of a hydrogen atom on the n-th orbit in electron volts, negative because the electron is bound, with -13.6 eV for the ground state
